options.a: Explain the bath is required by the care plan and proceed gently even if they object
options.b: Accept the refusal, skip the bath, and wait until the next visit to mention it to anyone
options.c: Call a family member to come over right away and persuade or help bathe the client despite their objection
options.d: Ask about concerns, offer choices (time/type), and report refusal per policy without forcing

distractorExplanations.a: Proceeding over an objection violates the client's right to refuse care, even when done gently and per the care plan.
distractorExplanations.b: Accepting the refusal is right, but it must be explored and reported per policy now, not held until a later visit.
distractorExplanations.c: Family pressure or assistance does not override a competent client's refusal; the aide offers choices and reports instead.

options.a: Retrains short-term memory and reverses cognitive decline in dementia
options.b: Keeps clients focused on the present by gently correcting inaccurate memories
options.c: Replaces the need for structured activities and social contact
options.d: Supports identity, mood, and cognitive engagement for many older adults

distractorExplanations.a: Overstates the benefit: reminiscence supports mood and identity but does not restore memory or reverse dementia.
distractorExplanations.b: Correcting the client toward the present is reality orientation; reminiscence invites past memories without correction.
distractorExplanations.c: Reminiscence is one psychosocial activity among many; it complements, not replaces, other activities and social contact.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-adls-00.explanation: Talking about life memories can support mood, identity, and engagement for many older adults when the client enjoys it. It does not reverse dementia, is not the same as correcting memories (reality orientation), and does not replace other activities or treatment.

options.a: Set a clear respectful boundary, state the behavior is inappropriate, and report per agency policy
options.b: Change the subject without comment and report it only if the comments become physical
options.c: Set a firm boundary, then end the visit and leave the home without notifying anyone
options.d: Ignore the comment because it may be a symptom of illness, and avoid documenting it to protect dignity

distractorExplanations.b: Verbal sexual harassment must be addressed with a boundary and reported; waiting for physical contact lets it escalate.
distractorExplanations.c: Leaving without notifying the supervisor can be client abandonment; the aide sets a boundary and reports per policy.
distractorExplanations.d: Even if behavior is illness-related, it must be redirected and documented/reported so the care team can plan for it.

options.a: Following the agency's standard daily schedule so every client gets equal care
options.b: Knowing the client’s preferences, routines, and life story to guide daily care
options.c: Letting family members decide daily routines because they know the client best
options.d: Doing tasks for the client to save energy, even ones they can still do alone

distractorExplanations.a: A uniform agency schedule is task-centered; person-centered care adapts routines to each client's preferences.
distractorExplanations.c: Family input helps, but person-centered care centers the client's own choices whenever the client can express them.
distractorExplanations.d: Doing tasks the client can manage undermines independence; person-centered care promotes self-care abilities.

options.a: Gives detailed medical explanations of every possible complication
options.b: Tells the client there is nothing to worry about and moves on quickly
options.c: Explains what will happen in simple terms and stays calm and supportive
options.d: Avoids mentioning the procedure until it starts so the client does not dwell on it

distractorExplanations.a: Detailed complication lists can increase fear and exceed aide scope; simple, calm explanations of what will happen reduce anxiety.
distractorExplanations.b: False reassurance brushes off the client's feelings; acknowledging concerns and explaining steps reduces anxiety.
distractorExplanations.d: Surprising the client increases fear and undermines consent; explaining beforehand in simple terms is the standard.

options.a: Giving medications and sterile invasive procedures not legally delegated
options.b: Reminding clients to take self-administered medications at scheduled times
options.c: Measuring and recording vital signs and weight as assigned in the care plan
options.d: Assisting with bathing, dressing, toileting, and transfers

distractorExplanations.b: Medication reminders for self-administering clients are generally within HHA scope; giving the medication itself is not.
distractorExplanations.c: Measuring assigned vital signs and weight is a standard HHA task, so it is inside the aide's scope.
distractorExplanations.d: ADL assistance such as bathing, dressing, toileting, and transfers is the core of HHA scope of practice.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-adls-00.explanation: HHAs assist with ADLs, assigned vitals, and supportive tasks under the care plan. Medication administration and invasive sterile procedures are generally outside HHA scope unless state law and training specifically authorize them. Some states allow specially trained, authorized aides to perform limited medication tasks.

options.a: Attempt it carefully after watching an online video demonstration first
options.b: Refuse politely, explain the limit, and notify the nurse or supervisor
options.c: Do it this one time if the client consents, then tell the supervisor later
options.d: Ask a more experienced aide on the team to do it for you instead

distractorExplanations.a: A video is not training or delegation; tasks beyond the aide's documented competency must be refused and escalated.
distractorExplanations.c: Client consent does not expand the aide's scope; the task must be refused and the supervisor notified first.
distractorExplanations.d: Another aide's experience does not authorize an out-of-scope task; the nurse or supervisor must reassign it.

options.a: Privacy and dignity, with care decisions left to the agency and family
options.b: Freedom from abuse, but not the right to refuse treatment ordered by a doctor
options.c: Privacy, dignity, freedom from abuse, and participation in care decisions
options.d: Unlimited services beyond the plan of care whenever the client asks

distractorExplanations.a: Clients have the right to participate in their own care planning; decisions are not handed to the agency and family.
distractorExplanations.b: Competent clients keep the right to refuse treatment, even when a physician ordered it.
distractorExplanations.d: Clients have rights to be informed about and participate in the plan of care, not to unlimited unplanned services.

options.a: Respecting a competent client's informed refusal of a bath and promptly reporting it to the nurse
options.b: Slapping or roughly handling a client during personal care
options.c: Using a client's bank card for the aide's own purchases without permission
options.d: Failing to provide needed care such as turning, fluids, or hygiene that creates a risk of harm

distractorExplanations.a: Honoring an informed refusal and reporting it is correct practice, not neglect, which is failure to provide needed care.
distractorExplanations.b: Hitting or rough handling is physical abuse (an act), whereas neglect is a failure to provide needed care.
distractorExplanations.c: Misusing a client's money is financial exploitation, a separate abuse category from neglect.

options.a: Gather proof over several visits first so the report will hold up
options.b: Ask the client and family members directly whether abuse is happening before making any report
options.c: Report it at the next scheduled team meeting so the supervisor can decide whether to act
options.d: Report immediately through the required chain and/or state hotline per agency policy and law

distractorExplanations.a: Mandatory reporters report reasonable suspicion promptly; proving abuse is the investigators' job, and delay risks harm.
distractorExplanations.b: Questioning the suspected household can endanger the client and tip off an abuser; report and let investigators interview.
distractorExplanations.c: Suspected abuse must be reported immediately, not held for a routine meeting, and the aide's duty is not delegated away.

options.a: Share client information with family members who ask, since they are close
options.b: Share client information only with those who need it to provide care
options.c: Discuss clients freely with coworkers at the agency, since all are staff
options.d: Share client details on social media if names and faces are left out

distractorExplanations.a: Family members get information only when the client authorizes it or they are part of care; closeness alone is not enough.
distractorExplanations.c: Being staff is not need-to-know; only those involved in the client's care should receive the information.
distractorExplanations.d: Details and photos can still identify a client; posting any client information on social media is a privacy breach.

options.a: Requested by family to prevent wandering, applied by the aide, and checked at the end of the visit
options.b: Ordered by a provider, applied as tightly as possible, and checked once per shift
options.c: Ordered by a provider, used as a last resort with the least restriction, and monitored per policy
options.d: The aide judges the client unsafe and applies it until the nurse can visit

distractorExplanations.a: Family requests do not authorize restraints; they need a provider order, least-restrictive use, and frequent monitoring.
distractorExplanations.b: Restraints must allow circulation and be checked frequently per policy, not applied tightly and checked once a shift.
distractorExplanations.d: Aides cannot decide to restrain a client; restraint requires a provider order and is a last resort.

options.a: Completed at the end of the week from memory to save visit time
options.b: Written in the aide's own interpretation of the client's mood and motives
options.c: Corrected by erasing or covering errors so the record stays neat
options.d: Objective, timely, correct, and free of blame or opinion language

distractorExplanations.a: Documentation must be timely, done at or near the time of care; weekly charting from memory is inaccurate.
distractorExplanations.b: Interpretations of mood and motives are subjective; charting records what was seen, heard, and measured.
distractorExplanations.c: Errors are corrected per policy (single line, initials, date), never erased or covered, which alters the legal record.

options.a: Answered promptly and kept within the client’s reach when in use
options.b: Kept in a central spot like the kitchen so the whole household can hear it
options.c: Answered promptly but stored in a drawer when the aide is in the home
options.d: Turned off during the aide's visit since the aide is already present

distractorExplanations.b: A device left in a central room may be out of the client's reach when they fall or need help; it must stay within reach.
distractorExplanations.c: Even with the aide present, the client needs the device within reach to summon help from another room.
distractorExplanations.d: Disabling the alert device removes the client's way to call for help if the aide is out of sight or an emergency occurs.

options.a: The client's physician, who handles home care service complaints and agency staffing disputes directly
options.b: The agency supervisor/compliance process and, when applicable, the state hotline or adult protective services
options.c: The aide personally, who should resolve the complaint quietly without involving the agency or the state
options.d: The client's health insurer, which must first approve any complaint before the agency is allowed to act on it

distractorExplanations.a: Physicians direct medical care, not agency service complaints; those go through the agency's grievance process or the state.
distractorExplanations.c: Aides must route complaints through the agency process; handling them privately blocks the client's right to a formal grievance.
distractorExplanations.d: No insurer approval is needed; clients may file directly with the agency and the state hotline or adult protective services.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-adls-01.explanation: Clients and families may raise concerns through the agency and, when needed, state complaint or adult protective services channels. Staff must not retaliate or try to settle complaints privately.

options.a: Report problems to the appropriate supervisor so issues are addressed safely
options.b: Report problems directly to the agency owner, bypassing the nurse supervisor
options.c: Solve problems on your own first and report only if they cannot be fixed
options.d: Report problems to the client's family, who then decide whether to tell the agency

distractorExplanations.b: Chain of command means going to the immediate supervisor first and moving up only if unresolved, not skipping levels.
distractorExplanations.c: Clinical and safety issues must be reported promptly; handling them alone delays care and exceeds aide scope.
distractorExplanations.d: Families are not part of the agency chain of command; problems go to the aide's supervisor or nurse.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-safety-.explanation: Use internal reporting pathways; emergencies still call for immediate help. Best answer: Report problems to the appropriate supervisor so issues are addressed safely. Home safety and infection control protect both the client and the aide; follow agency policy and escalate hazards promptly.

options.a: Takes a scheduled break after giving report and arranging coverage
options.b: Leaves an assigned shift/clients without giving report or being relieved
options.c: Refuses an unsafe task, notifies the supervisor, and continues other care
options.d: Ends the visit on time after completing assigned care and documenting it

distractorExplanations.a: A break with report and coverage arranged is a proper handoff, so it is not abandonment.
distractorExplanations.c: Refusing an unsafe task while staying and reporting is appropriate; abandonment means leaving clients without relief.
distractorExplanations.d: Leaving at the scheduled end after completing care is normal; abandonment is leaving an assignment without report or relief.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-safety-.explanation: Leaving without relief endangers clients. Best answer: Leaves an assigned shift/clients without giving report or being relieved. Home safety and infection control protect both the client and the aide; follow agency policy and escalate hazards promptly.

options.a: “Client seemed upset at lunch and probably has the stomach flu again; vomited a lot.”
options.b: “Client ate poorly, complained a lot, and vomited a large amount.”
options.c: “Client ate 50% of lunch; stated abdominal pain 6/10; vomited 100 mL green fluid.”
options.d: “Client refused most of lunch because she is depressed and vomited afterward.”

distractorExplanations.a: Mixes an assumed diagnosis and vague amounts; objective notes give measured intake, the client's quote, and output in mL.
distractorExplanations.b: “Poorly,” “a lot,” and “a large amount” are vague judgments; objective charting uses percentages, ratings, and mL.
distractorExplanations.d: Attributing the refusal to depression is an interpretation (a diagnosis); aides record observable facts and quotes.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-safety-.explanation: Chart facts and quotes; avoid judgmental labels. Best answer: “Client ate 50% of lunch; stated abdominal pain 6/10; vomited 100 mL green fluid.”. Home safety and infection control protect both the client and the aide; follow agency policy and escalate hazards promptly.

options.a: Use hand hygiene and appropriate PPE for all clients as indicated
options.b: Use gloves and gowns only for clients with a known infection diagnosis
options.c: Wear gloves for all care so handwashing can be skipped between tasks
options.d: Use PPE when the client looks ill, and wash hands at the end of each visit

distractorExplanations.b: Standard precautions apply to every client because infections are often undiagnosed; diagnosis-based PPE is transmission-based.
distractorExplanations.c: Gloves do not replace hand hygiene; hands are cleaned before and after glove use.
distractorExplanations.d: Appearance does not predict infection, and hand hygiene is needed at multiple moments, not once per visit.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-safety-.explanation: Treat all blood/body fluids as potentially infectious. Best answer: Use hand hygiene and appropriate PPE for all clients as indicated. Home safety and infection control protect both the client and the aide; follow agency policy and escalate hazards promptly.

distractorExplanations.a: That range is hypothermia, well below the normal adult oral temperature of about 97.6–99.6°F.
distractorExplanations.b: That range is below normal and would be reported as possible hypothermia or a measurement error.
distractorExplanations.d: 100.4°F (38°C) and above is a fever that should be reported, not a normal temperature.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-safety-.explanation: Know agency normal ranges and report fever/hypothermia promptly. Best answer: 97.6°F to 99.6°F (about 36.5–37.5°C). Home safety and infection control protect both the client and the aide; follow agency policy and escalate hazards promptly.

options.a: Wrist on the thumb side
options.b: Wrist on the little-finger side
options.c: Inner elbow above the crease
options.d: Top of the foot

distractorExplanations.b: The little-finger side of the wrist is the ulnar artery; the radial pulse is on the thumb side.
distractorExplanations.c: The inner elbow is the brachial pulse site, used for blood pressure, not the radial pulse.
distractorExplanations.d: The top of the foot is the dorsalis pedis pulse; the radial pulse is felt at the thumb side of the wrist.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-safety-.explanation: Radial is the common aide pulse site; report irregular/weak pulses. Best answer: Wrist on the thumb side. Home safety and infection control protect both the client and the aide; follow agency policy and escalate hazards promptly.

options.a: 128/82 mm Hg in a client who reports mild fatigue after a large lunch
options.b: 188/110 mm Hg in a client who is symptomatic or per agency thresholds
options.c: 138/88 mm Hg just after the client walked quickly to answer the door
options.d: 92/58 mm Hg in a client whose baseline is usually low-normal

distractorExplanations.a: 128/82 is elevated/stage 1 range at most and not a severe reading needing immediate report on its own.
distractorExplanations.c: Mildly high readings after activity are expected; recheck after rest rather than treat as a severe emergency.
distractorExplanations.d: This is low, not high, and near this client's baseline; the question asks about an abnormally high reading.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-safety-.explanation: Know client baselines and agency report parameters; severe hypertension needs prompt nursing notification. Best answer: 188/110 mm Hg in a client who is symptomatic or per agency thresholds. Home safety and infection control protect both the client and the aide; follow agency policy and escalate hazards promptly.

options.a: Wear an N95 respirator and keep the client in a negative-pressure room
options.b: Wear gloves and a gown for any contact with the client or surfaces
options.c: Wear a mask when working within close range of the client as directed
options.d: Wear a mask only when the client is coughing during the visit

distractorExplanations.a: N95 and negative-pressure rooms are airborne precautions (e.g., TB, measles), not droplet precautions.
distractorExplanations.b: Gloves and gown for any contact describe contact precautions; droplet precautions center on a mask at close range.
distractorExplanations.d: Droplet precautions apply whenever working close to the client per the isolation order, not only during coughing.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-safety-.explanation: Follow the isolation sign and nurse instructions for PPE. Best answer: Wear a mask when working within close range of the client as directed. Home safety and infection control protect both the client and the aide; follow agency policy and escalate hazards promptly.

options.a: Rolled up and carried against the uniform so that nothing drops onto the floor
options.b: Shaken out first to remove debris, then placed in the laundry bag
options.c: Placed on the floor in a neat pile until the bed is finished
options.d: Held away from the uniform and placed in appropriate bags; never shaken

distractorExplanations.a: Carrying soiled linen against the uniform contaminates clothing; it is held away from the body.
distractorExplanations.b: Shaking dirty linen spreads microorganisms into the air; linen is rolled inward and bagged without shaking.
distractorExplanations.c: The floor is contaminated and linen there spreads germs; soiled linen goes directly into a bag or hamper.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-safety-.explanation: Linen handling prevents environmental contamination. Best answer: Held away from the uniform and placed in appropriate bags; never shaken. Home safety and infection control protect both the client and the aide; follow agency policy and escalate hazards promptly.

options.a: Nail polish, poor perfusion, or motion interferes with the sensor
options.b: The client has just eaten or drunk a hot beverage before the reading
options.c: The client is sitting upright instead of lying flat in bed
options.d: The cuff is too small or placed over clothing on the upper arm

distractorExplanations.b: Recent hot drinks affect oral temperature readings, not pulse oximetry, which reads light absorption at the fingertip.
distractorExplanations.c: Upright positioning does not invalidate SpO2; motion, nail polish, and poor perfusion are the main sources of error.
distractorExplanations.d: Cuff size and placement affect blood pressure readings; a pulse oximeter uses a finger or ear sensor, not a cuff.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-safety-.explanation: Report unexpected SpO2 values and recheck technique/site. Best answer: Nail polish, poor perfusion, or motion interferes with the sensor. Home safety and infection control protect both the client and the aide; follow agency policy and escalate hazards promptly.

options.a: Weigh the client at any convenient time of day, as long as the scale is zeroed
options.b: Balance/zero the scale, use consistent clothing/footwear approach, and assist for safety
options.c: Have the client wear outdoor shoes and a coat for stability, then subtract an estimated amount
options.d: Compare the reading with the last weight and round it to match if close

distractorExplanations.a: Weights are compared over time, so they are taken at the same time of day with similar clothing, not whenever convenient.
distractorExplanations.c: Estimating clothing weight introduces error; the approach to clothing and footwear must be consistent each time.
distractorExplanations.d: Adjusting a reading to match the last value falsifies data and can hide fluid gain the nurse needs to see.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-safety-.explanation: Accurate weights guide clinical decisions (heart failure, nutrition). Best answer: Balance/zero the scale, use consistent clothing/footwear approach, and assist for safety. Home safety and infection control protect both the client and the aide; follow agency policy and escalate hazards promptly.

options.a: Hands are visibly soiled after helping with toileting
options.b: After caring for a client with C. difficile diarrhea
options.c: Hands are not visibly soiled and agency policy allows it
options.d: After hands contact blood, as long as gloves were not worn

distractorExplanations.a: Visibly soiled hands require soap and water; alcohol rub does not remove physical soil.
distractorExplanations.b: Alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores; soap and water handwashing is required per policy.
distractorExplanations.d: Blood on bare hands is visible contamination that requires soap and water washing, not alcohol rub.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-safety-.explanation: Soap/water for visible soil and spore-forming organisms per policy (e.g., C. diff). Best answer: Hands are not visibly soiled and agency policy allows it. Home safety and infection control protect both the client and the aide; follow agency policy and escalate hazards promptly.

options.a: Remove the mask first so you can breathe freely, then the gloves and gown
options.b: Remove gloves last after the gown and mask, then perform hand hygiene
options.c: Perform hand hygiene only at the start of the visit, then remove the PPE items in any order you like
options.d: Remove the most contaminated items first in the taught order, then perform hand hygiene

distractorExplanations.a: The mask is removed last (after leaving the area); gloves, the most contaminated item, come off first.
distractorExplanations.b: Gloves are the most contaminated item and are removed first (or with the gown), not after the mask.
distractorExplanations.c: Doffing follows a set order to avoid self-contamination, and hand hygiene is required after PPE removal.

options.a: Treat every client exactly the same way so that no culture receives special treatment
options.b: Use family members as interpreters for medical information to save time
options.c: Respect preferences about food, touch, privacy, and end-of-life customs within agency rules
options.d: Assume the client's food and end-of-life preferences from their ethnic background without asking

distractorExplanations.a: Identical treatment ignores individual needs; cultural sensitivity adapts care to each client's preferences.
distractorExplanations.b: Family interpreters can filter or distort information and breach privacy; use qualified interpreters per agency policy.
distractorExplanations.d: Stereotyping by background is not cultural sensitivity; preferences vary by individual and should be asked about.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-obs-001.explanation: Person-centered care includes cultural humility. Best answer: Respect preferences about food, touch, privacy, and end-of-life customs within agency rules. Observe, document objectively, and report changes to the nurse or supervisor—do not diagnose or delay urgent concerns.

options.a: Reassure the client that everything will be fine and quickly change the subject to cheer them up
options.b: Give the client privacy by leaving to finish housework, and check back at the end of the visit
options.c: Ask for details about the call so you can advise the client on how best to resolve the family conflict
options.d: Sit with the client, offer presence, and ask if they want to talk or have the nurse/supervisor notified

distractorExplanations.a: False reassurance and changing the subject dismiss the client's feelings; supportive presence and listening are the aim.
distractorExplanations.b: Leaving for the rest of the visit misses emotional support and observation; offer presence and ask what the client wants.
distractorExplanations.c: Probing and giving advice on family conflict exceed the aide role; listen if the client wants to talk and report concerns.

options.a: Respected as a normal human need within consent, privacy, and safety policies
options.b: Discouraged in clients over 75 because it raises the risk of falls and injury
options.c: Ignored by the aide even when public behavior needs gentle redirection
options.d: Reported to the family each time the client expresses a romantic interest

distractorExplanations.b: Age is not a reason to discourage sexuality; it remains a normal need within consent, privacy, and safety.
distractorExplanations.c: Inappropriate public behavior should be redirected and reported professionally, not ignored.
distractorExplanations.d: Sharing a competent adult's romantic interests with family breaches privacy; only safety or consent concerns go to the nurse.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-obs-003.explanation: Address inappropriate behavior professionally; support privacy for appropriate consensual expression per policy. Best answer: Respected as a normal human need within consent, privacy, and safety policies. Observe, document objectively, and report changes to the nurse or supervisor—do not diagnose or delay urgent concerns.

options.a: Speak loudly and slowly with exaggerated mouth movements while standing to the side of the client's good ear
options.b: Face the client, speak clearly at a moderate pace, reduce background noise, and use assistive devices
options.c: Raise your voice to a near-shout and repeat the same words until the client understands
options.d: Speak into the hearing aid ear from behind so the device picks up your voice directly

distractorExplanations.a: Exaggerated mouthing distorts lip-reading cues, and standing to the side hides the face; face the client and speak clearly.
distractorExplanations.c: Shouting distorts sound; rephrase rather than repeat, speak at moderate volume, and reduce background noise.
distractorExplanations.d: Speaking from behind removes visual cues; face the client so they can see your lips and expressions.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-obs-004.explanation: Communication adaptations reduce isolation. Best answer: Face the client, speak clearly at a moderate pace, reduce background noise, and use assistive devices. Observe, document objectively, and report changes to the nurse or supervisor—do not diagnose or delay urgent concerns.

options.a: Moves the client's belongings to new, more convenient spots so they do not have to reach as far
options.b: Guides the client by holding their arm and pushing them ahead of the aide
options.c: Identifies self when entering, explains care before touching, and keeps pathways clear
options.d: Arranges food randomly on the tray and lets the client find it by touch

distractorExplanations.a: Clients with vision loss rely on items staying in familiar places; moving them causes confusion and falls.
distractorExplanations.b: In sighted guide technique the client holds the aide's arm and walks slightly behind, not pushed ahead.
distractorExplanations.d: Food is described using the clock method so the client can locate items; random placement removes independence.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-obs-005.explanation: Consistency and verbal cueing support independence and safety. Best answer: Identifies self when entering, explains care before touching, and keeps pathways clear. Observe, document objectively, and report changes to the nurse or supervisor—do not diagnose or delay urgent concerns.

options.a: Normal age-related changes in vision, hearing, and taste in older adults
options.b: Stages of grief such as denial, anger, and bargaining in terminal illness
options.c: Circulatory problems that affect blood pressure, pulse, and skin color
options.d: Neurologic changes that affect recognition, language, and skilled movement

distractorExplanations.a: Agnosia, aphasia, and apraxia are neurologic deficits (e.g., after stroke or dementia), not normal sensory aging.
distractorExplanations.b: Denial, anger, and bargaining are Kübler-Ross grief stages; these terms describe recognition, language, and movement deficits.
distractorExplanations.c: These terms describe brain-based cognitive and communication deficits, not cardiovascular or circulatory problems.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-obs-006.explanation: Understanding cognitive/communication deficits improves care and reduces agitation. Best answer: Neurologic changes that affect recognition, language, and skilled movement. Observe, document objectively, and report changes to the nurse or supervisor—do not diagnose or delay urgent concerns. These deficits require patience and adapted communication.

options.a: Keeping the TV or radio on all day to fill the quiet in the home
options.b: Encouraging appropriate social contact and meaningful conversation
options.c: Limiting visitors so the client can rest and avoid overstimulation
options.d: Completing hobbies for the client so they do not tire themselves out

distractorExplanations.a: Background noise is not social connection and may not match preferences; meaningful contact reduces loneliness.
distractorExplanations.c: Restricting visitors increases isolation; appropriate social contact is encouraged unless the care plan says otherwise.
distractorExplanations.d: Doing hobbies for the client removes the meaningful engagement that reduces loneliness; support their participation.

options.a: To let the aide raise or lower the client's ordered fluid restriction as needed
options.b: To replace daily weights as the main way the team measures fluid status
options.c: To calculate the client's calorie intake for the dietitian
options.d: To help the care team track fluid balance and notice concerning changes

distractorExplanations.a: Aides measure and report I&O; changing a fluid restriction is a clinical decision for the nurse or provider.
distractorExplanations.b: I&O complements daily weights; both are tracked, and one does not replace the other.
distractorExplanations.c: Calorie counts are a separate record; I&O tracks fluid volumes in and out to monitor fluid balance.

options.a: Sudden confusion, new shortness of breath, or a fall with possible injury
options.b: A client with known dementia repeating the same story several times
options.c: A small decrease in appetite at one meal after a large late breakfast
options.d: Mild stiffness on rising that eases after the client starts moving

distractorExplanations.b: Repetition consistent with the client's known baseline is not an acute change; sudden new confusion is.
distractorExplanations.c: A single small, explainable drop in appetite is not urgent; sudden or persistent changes would be reported.
distractorExplanations.d: Brief morning stiffness that resolves with movement is a common baseline finding, not an urgent change.

options.a: Massage the red area with lotion to restore circulation before reporting it
options.b: Report the finding promptly and follow pressure-relief instructions in the care plan
options.c: Recheck it at the next visit, since redness usually fades on its own within a day or two
options.d: Apply a heating pad to increase blood flow and document it at shift's end

distractorExplanations.a: Massaging reddened bony areas damages tissue further; non-blanching redness is reported and offloaded, not rubbed.
distractorExplanations.c: Non-blanching redness is a stage 1 pressure injury sign and must be reported promptly, not watched until later.
distractorExplanations.d: Heat is not an aide intervention for pressure injury and can burn fragile skin; report promptly instead.

options.a: Ask the client what they would like and prepare it, since preferences come first
options.b: Position the client semi-reclined at about 30 degrees to make swallowing easier
options.c: Check the care plan for diet orders, allergies, and swallowing precautions
options.d: Cut all food into small pieces and thicken liquids for every older client

distractorExplanations.a: Preferences matter, but diet orders, allergies, and swallowing precautions must be checked before any food is offered.
distractorExplanations.b: A semi-reclined position increases aspiration risk; clients eat sitting upright (about 90 degrees) unless ordered otherwise.
distractorExplanations.d: Texture changes and thickened liquids are ordered for specific clients, not applied to every older adult.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-obs-013.explanation: Meal assistance must follow diet, allergy, and dysphagia orders. Upright positioning as directed reduces aspiration risk. Do not improvise food or seasonings against the care plan. Then position the client upright as directed.

options.a: Lock the wheelchair brakes and ensure nonskid footwear if used
options.b: Raise the bed to its highest position so the client can slide down
options.c: Place the wheelchair facing away from the bed at the foot end
options.d: Remove the footrests after the client is seated to avoid tripping

distractorExplanations.b: The bed is lowered so the client's feet are flat on the floor; a high bed increases fall risk during transfer.
distractorExplanations.c: The wheelchair is placed beside the bed at a slight angle on the client's stronger side, not away at the foot end.
distractorExplanations.d: Footrests are swung away before the transfer and replaced after seating; removing them afterward is backward.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-obs-014.explanation: Brakes, footwear, bed height, and clear communication prevent falls. Best answer: Lock the wheelchair brakes and ensure nonskid footwear if used. Observe, document objectively, and report changes to the nurse or supervisor—do not diagnose or delay urgent concerns.

options.a: Pull the client toward you by the arm and shoulder in one quick motion
options.b: Use draw sheets/assistance and keep the spine in alignment per care plan
options.c: Turn the shoulders first, then the hips once the upper body is on its side
options.d: Raise the head of the bed to 90 degrees before rolling the client

distractorExplanations.a: Pulling by a limb strains joints and shears skin; a draw sheet and help move the body as one unit.
distractorExplanations.c: Turning shoulders before hips twists the spine; logrolling moves shoulders and hips together in alignment.
distractorExplanations.d: Turning is done with the bed flat (or as ordered); a raised head of bed makes alignment and turning harder.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-obs-015.explanation: Logrolling/assistance protects skin and musculoskeletal injury. Best answer: Use draw sheets/assistance and keep the spine in alignment per care plan. Observe, document objectively, and report changes to the nurse or supervisor—do not diagnose or delay urgent concerns.

options.a: Explain that safety concerns must be reported to the nurse/supervisor, then report the symptoms
options.b: Respect the request because confidentiality means the client alone controls all of their health information
options.c: Tell the client to stop the medication until the nurse visits next week
options.d: Wait to report it until the side effect is still present at the end of the visit

distractorExplanations.b: Confidentiality limits sharing outside the care team; it does not allow hiding safety concerns from the nurse.
distractorExplanations.c: Advising a client to stop a medication is outside aide scope and could cause harm; report to the nurse now.
distractorExplanations.d: New medication side effects are reported promptly, not delayed to see whether they persist.

options.a: Accepting small cash gifts from the client, since refusing them could damage the trust in the relationship
options.b: Keeping relationships professional, declining personal gifts/loans, and following agency boundary policy
options.c: Sharing personal phone numbers with the client so they can reach the aide directly outside work hours
options.d: Agreeing to become the client's power of attorney when the family lives too far away to help in person

distractorExplanations.a: Cash gifts create a boundary and exploitation risk; aides follow agency gift policy and generally decline them.
distractorExplanations.c: Off-duty contact blurs the professional role; clients contact the agency for needs outside visit times.
distractorExplanations.d: Serving as power of attorney is a dual relationship and conflict of interest for a paid aide.

options.a: Share any client information freely with relatives who call the home, since family has a right to know
options.b: Discuss client cases with coworkers by name at the agency office, since everyone there is staff
options.c: Share only need-to-know information with authorized care-team members and protect records/conversations
options.d: Keep records private, but post client photos online when the client's face is not shown

distractorExplanations.a: Family members do not automatically have a right to PHI; the client's authorization or care role is required.
distractorExplanations.b: HIPAA's minimum-necessary rule limits sharing to staff involved in the client's care, not everyone at the agency.
distractorExplanations.d: Photos can still identify a client through the home or details; posting client images online is a privacy breach.

options.a: Refuse, explain medication is outside the aide’s role, and notify the nurse/supervisor
options.b: Give it because a family caregiver is allowed to delegate medication tasks to the home health aide
options.c: Give it only if the client agrees and the dose matches the bottle label
options.d: Refuse, but show the family how to give it themselves without telling the nurse

distractorExplanations.b: Family members cannot delegate medication administration to an aide; delegation comes from the nurse within state law.
distractorExplanations.c: Client agreement and a matching label do not make it an ordered medication or put administration in aide scope.
distractorExplanations.d: Refusing is right, but the nurse must be told; teaching medication administration is also outside aide scope.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-ethics-.explanation: HHAs follow the care plan and scope of practice. Unauthorized medication administration is dangerous and must be refused and reported. Some states authorize specially trained aides for limited medication tasks, but only under the care plan.

options.a: Follow agency routines first and accommodate cultural practices only when time allows during visits
options.b: Ask about preferences that affect care (food, privacy, language, religious practices) and adapt within the care plan
options.c: Learn general facts about the client's culture and apply them without asking about individual personal preferences
options.d: Adapt to every cultural request, including changes to diet orders or medications the client asks for

distractorExplanations.a: Cultural preferences that affect care are built into the care plan, not treated as optional extras when time allows.
distractorExplanations.c: General cultural facts can become stereotypes; cultural respect means asking the individual about their preferences.
distractorExplanations.d: Adaptations stay within the care plan; diet orders and medications are changed only by the nurse or provider.

options.a: Lift a fallen client off the floor by the belt alone without help
options.b: Keep a client seated safely in a chair while the aide does housework
options.c: Provide a secure hold to assist ambulation/transfers when appropriate
options.d: Support a client's lower back as a brace during long periods of standing

distractorExplanations.a: Gait belts assist ambulation and transfers; lifting a fallen client needs assessment, help, or a mechanical lift.
distractorExplanations.b: Using a belt to keep a client in a chair makes it a restraint, which requires an order and is not its purpose.
distractorExplanations.d: A gait belt is a handling aid for the caregiver's grip, not a lumbar support brace for the client.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-ethics-.explanation: Gait belts aid safe mobility; they are not punitive restraints. Best answer: Provide a secure hold to assist ambulation/transfers when appropriate. Stay in scope: protect privacy, refuse illegal or unsafe requests, and use the chain of command for clinical issues.

options.a: Positioning flat on the back and rinsing the mouth with a cup of water
options.b: Skipping mouth care since an unconscious client does not eat or drink
options.c: Using lemon-glycerin swabs routinely to keep the mouth moist and fresh
options.d: Positioning on the side, using swabs per protocol, and protecting the airway

distractorExplanations.a: Supine positioning with rinse water risks aspiration; unconscious clients are positioned on the side with minimal fluid.
distractorExplanations.b: Unconscious clients need frequent mouth care because mouth breathing and no oral intake dry and damage the mucosa.
distractorExplanations.c: Lemon-glycerin swabs dry and irritate the mucosa and are generally avoided; use swabs and solutions per protocol.

options.a: Massage reddened bony areas firmly with lotion to stimulate circulation and prevent breakdown
options.b: Reposition immobile clients at least every 2 hours (or per care plan) and keep skin clean/dry
options.c: Reposition immobile clients every 4 to 6 hours to allow uninterrupted rest and sleep
options.d: Keep the head of the bed raised above 60 degrees to reduce pressure on the sacrum

distractorExplanations.a: Massaging reddened bony prominences damages tissue; prevention relies on repositioning and moisture control.
distractorExplanations.c: A 4- to 6-hour interval is too long; immobile clients are repositioned at least every 2 hours or per the care plan.
distractorExplanations.d: A high head of bed increases sacral pressure and shear; keep it at or below 30 degrees unless ordered otherwise.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-ethics-.explanation: Pressure relief and moisture control are core prevention strategies. Best answer: Reposition immobile clients at least every 2 hours (or per care plan) and keep skin clean/dry. Stay in scope: protect privacy, refuse illegal or unsafe requests, and use the chain of command for clinical issues.

options.a: Pull the client up by the armpits, since that keeps the hips off the sheet
options.b: Raise the head of the bed higher first so the client can push up alone
options.c: Use proper lift/assist techniques and enough help; avoid dragging the skin
options.d: Slide the client up on the bottom sheet quickly to limit time in motion

distractorExplanations.a: Pulling under the arms injures shoulders and still drags the skin; use a draw sheet with enough help.
distractorExplanations.b: Raising the head of the bed makes the client slide further; lower it flat (as tolerated) before moving up.
distractorExplanations.d: Sliding drags skin against the sheet and causes shear; the draw sheet is lifted, not slid, with assistance.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-ethics-.explanation: Shearing contributes to pressure injuries; use draw sheets and teamwork. Best answer: Use proper lift/assist techniques and enough help; avoid dragging the skin. Stay in scope: protect privacy, refuse illegal or unsafe requests, and use the chain of command for clinical issues.

options.a: From back to front for females, using clean areas of the washcloth, maintaining privacy and dignity
options.b: From front to back for females, reusing the same washcloth area to limit linen use and save time
options.c: In circular motions starting at the anus and moving outward for both male and female clients
options.d: From front to back for females, using clean areas of the washcloth, maintaining privacy and dignity

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the direction: wiping back to front carries bowel bacteria toward the urethra and raises UTI risk.
distractorExplanations.b: Reusing the same area spreads contamination; a clean section of the washcloth is used for each stroke.
distractorExplanations.c: Starting at the anus spreads fecal bacteria; perineal care moves from cleanest (urethra) to dirtiest (anal area).

home-health-aide-readiness-check-ethics-.explanation: Front-to-back reduces UTI risk; standard precautions and privacy apply. Best answer: From front to back for females, using clean areas of the washcloth, maintaining privacy and dignity. Stay in scope: protect privacy, refuse illegal or unsafe requests, and use the chain of command for clinical issues.

options.a: Control the fall and lower the client gently to the floor protecting the head, then call for help
options.b: Catch the client under the arms and hold them upright until the fall stops, then reseat them
options.c: Lower the client to the floor, then help them stand right away so they do not stay on the floor for long
options.d: Pull the client back toward you by the gait belt to keep them standing at all costs

distractorExplanations.b: Trying to hold a falling client upright injures both people; the aide guides the client down to the floor.
distractorExplanations.c: After a fall the client stays down until checked and help arrives; getting them up immediately can worsen injury.
distractorExplanations.d: Pulling against a fall strains the aide's back and can injure the client; the belt is used to ease them down.

options.a: Performed past the point of mild pain, since slight discomfort shows the stretch is working
options.b: Performed as ordered, supporting joints, stopping if pain occurs, and reporting changes
options.c: Performed quickly with as many repetitions as tolerated, without needing to support joints
options.d: Performed on every joint including any the care plan restricts, to prevent contractures

distractorExplanations.a: ROM stops at the point of pain or resistance; pushing past pain risks joint and soft-tissue injury.
distractorExplanations.c: ROM is done slowly, gently, with joints supported, for the number of repetitions in the care plan.
distractorExplanations.d: Joints the care plan restricts (e.g., after surgery) are not exercised; follow the ordered ROM only.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-ethics-.explanation: ROM preserves mobility; never force through pain; follow care plan. Best answer: Performed as ordered, supporting joints, stopping if pain occurs, and reporting changes. Stay in scope: protect privacy, refuse illegal or unsafe requests, and use the chain of command for clinical issues.

options.a: Only at scheduled times so the client gets used to a routine
options.b: With the client lying flat so the pan stays level beneath them
options.c: With privacy, proper positioning, and hand hygiene before/after
options.d: With gloves on, which replaces the need for hand hygiene after

distractorExplanations.a: Toileting help is offered when the client needs it as well as on schedule; withholding it risks incontinence and skin damage.
distractorExplanations.b: The head of the bed is raised (as allowed) to a sitting position for comfort and natural elimination.
distractorExplanations.d: Gloves do not replace hand hygiene; hands are cleaned after glove removal.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-ethics-.explanation: Elimination assistance requires dignity and infection control. Best answer: With privacy, proper positioning, and hand hygiene before/after. Stay in scope: protect privacy, refuse illegal or unsafe requests, and use the chain of command for clinical issues.

options.a: Remove the top linen fully so the client can be turned quickly and the bed made faster
options.b: Roll the client toward the open side without a raised rail or helper while tucking the far side
options.c: Gather dirty linen and shake it out over the floor before placing it in the hamper
options.d: Keep the client covered for privacy/warmth and use side rails per policy for safety during turning

distractorExplanations.a: Exposing the client breaks privacy and causes chilling; a bath blanket or top sheet keeps them covered.
distractorExplanations.b: Turning toward an unguarded side risks a fall; the client is turned toward a raised rail or a helper per policy.
distractorExplanations.c: Shaking soiled linen spreads microorganisms; it is rolled inward and bagged without shaking.

home-health-aide-readiness-check-ethics-.explanation: Occupied bedmaking maintains safety, dignity, and infection control. Best answer: Keep the client covered for privacy/warmth and use side rails per policy for safety during turning. Stay in scope: protect privacy, refuse illegal or unsafe requests, and use the chain of command for clinical issues.
